A lack of rainfall linked to El Niño has affected the water levels in the canal, resulting in officials reducing daily vessel traffic. Photograph: Enea Lebrun/Reuters View image in fullscreen A Liberian-flagged container ship transits the Panama canal. A lack of rainfall linked to El Niño has affected the water levels in the canal, resulting in officials reducing daily vessel traffic. Photograph: Enea Lebrun/Reuters Panama canal Panama canal traffic to be cut again as drought from El Niño worsens Latest daily reductions will further choke one of the world’s most important shipping lanes Mark Saunokonoko with Agence France-Presse Mon 14 Sep 2026 22.43 EDT Last modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 22.44 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The Panama canal plans to again cut maritime traffic due to worsening drought caused by the El Niño climate phenomenon, further choking up one of the world’s most important shipping lanes. The canal handles 5% of global maritime trade and about 40% of US container traffic; it is favoured by shippers because it usually reduces cost and transit times, especially for companies trading between China, Asia and the US. From October, an average of 29.5 vessels will be allowed to transit daily – down 18% from 36 in August, according to a draft plan submitted to Panama’s parliament. In September, officials cut daily transits from 36 to 32 because of the drought. How Panama canal connects the Caribbean Sea to the Pacific Ocean The US and Israel’s war on Iran, and its disruption to the strait of Hormuz, has complicated logistics and added costs for shipping companies using the canal. In August, with vessels waiting 10 days to enter the canal – the longest since May – a container ship reportedly paid about $4m (£3m) to jump the queue. Maritime companies usually pay a flat fee to reserve a slot to transit the canal, but a daily auction allows shipowners to place bids to skip the queue. Bid prices generally rise during high demand. Shipping restrictions on the canal could yet worsen, with El Niño expected to peak later this year. The natural weather pattern that brings worldwide changes in winds, air pressure and rainfall patterns is forecast to be the strongest in four decades. The 82km-long canal, connecting the Caribbean Sea to the Pacific Ocean, relies on fresh water from rivers pouring into Lake Gatun to operate its system of locks. In September, officials said the watershed had received lower than forecast rainfall. The canal’s locks act like elevators, each filling with water to lift ships 26 metres (85 feet) from sea level to Lake Gatun and then back down to sea level on the other side. If lake levels are no longer safe for the largest ships to pass, the Panama Canal Authority imposes restrictions for safety and to preserve water. In 2023 the water level in the lakes feeding the canal was so low authorities cut daily transits from 38 to 22. Those restrictions led to a bottleneck of ships and sent companies scrambling to find alternative routes . El Niño has severely affected Central America and northern parts of South America, where nine countries have experienced their hottest June-August period on record this year. Panama canal to reduce shipping as El Niño strikes vital route Read more Fifty-two countries across all continents broke their seasonal temperature records for that period, according to an Agence France-Presse analysis of meteorological data from the European Copernicus programme. The extreme heat has taken many forms, from unprecedented heatwaves in Europe to devastating drought in Sudan and toxic smoke in Indonesia . More than a third of people experiencing the hottest northern summer months on record were in Africa, particularly in the Sahel and areas south of it. Eighteen African countries broke their seasonal records for the June-August period, from Mauritania and Sierra Leone in the west to Eritrea and Ethiopia in the east. https://www.politico.eu/article/nato-cha.text: BRUSSELS — NATO’s most senior commanders elect a new leader on Saturday in a consequential vote that will help shape how the alliance prepares for a potential Russian incursion and navigates persisting transatlantic tensions. The alliance’s 32 chiefs of defense staff will elect a new chair of NATO’s most senior military body, the military committee, in Copenhagen in a hush-hush ballot — and choose between two candidates: Germany’s Gen. Carsten Breuer and Canada’s Gen. Jennie Carignan. “NATO is in a very decisive moment and in a demanding spot — there’s a large conventional war raging in Europe and NATO is transforming itself again into a more robust, more European NATO,” said Janne Kuusela, Permanent Secretary at the Finnish defense ministry. “That of course means … we need the best possible individuals to fill these positions.” Advertisement Advertisement Although little-known, NATO’s military committee is the alliance’s most senior military authority, with the chair expected to give honest military advice to allies — helping assess the feasibility, financing and capabilities of operations. They oversee dozens of working groups of NATO military staff, and broker consensus on formulating military advice. The position is a “highly complex role,” said Eleonora Russell, the spokesperson of former chair Adm. Rob Bauer, because it requires simultaneously gaining the trust of both the military and the political leadership across the alliance — and not taking sides. Such a role is particularly challenging today given enduring transatlantic tensions, she said, and important as sensitive talks on NATO’s next four-year war planning cycle will kick off in October. “The trick is you have to be … an extremely good listener,” Russell said, “but then you have to also have a very strong backbone.” Germany’s Breuer, who Berlin announced as a candidate in February, is seen as the front-runner, according to one NATO diplomat and two European national security officials, who were granted anonymity to speak freely about the sensitive matter. Berlin is now Europe’s leading defense spender , the officials said, and the U.S. has previously nudged Germany toward leadership roles in the alliance as it seeks to reduce its military engagement on the continent. Strained bilateral ties between Ottawa and Washington might also make Carignan’s case more difficult, the officials said. That support was on display in Washington on Jul. 23, when Breuer briefed Pentagon policy chief Elbridge Colby on Germany’s new military strategy. Colby later called the strategy “historic” and “highly laudable” and said Germany was positioning itself as “a key leader of Europe’s conventional defense” in a post on X . Advertisement Advertisement “Both candidates are exceptional military leaders,” said another military official, who nonetheless wondered whether it was more important today to have a European in charge given the alliance’s push for the continent to take charge of its own defense, dubbed NATO 3.0. Breuer’s pitch for the job has included its leadership role on NATO 3.0, the officials said, as well as the four-star general’s strong existing relationships with his counterparts since he took over as Germany’s chief of defense in 2023. Carignan, Ottawa’s top general since 2024, has focused her campaign on reinvigorating the role of the military committee, the officials said, and signaling enduring transatlantic unity inside NATO. That comes as the alliance has repeatedly been rocked by feuds with U.S. President Donald Trump since he retook office last year. Germany’s defense ministry didn’t respond to a request for comment. A spokesperson for Canada’s defense ministry said Carignan’s “candidacy reflects Canada's enduring commitment to NATO and to strengthening collective defence and transatlantic security.” Out of sight, out of mind Yet the campaign is enigmatic and behind closed doors — all the way down to the blind vote. That’s because “the whole point of this is for this to be a military group of professionals who trust each other,” Russell said, since “on the military level you need to have boundless loyalty, and if you know exactly who voted for you and who didn't, then you lose that.” Advertisement Advertisement To ensure that loyalty, the vote count will stop once a majority — or 17 votes — is reached, leaving the real result unknown, one NATO official said. Adding to the mystery, some chiefs of defense are under strict instructions by their ministries to vote for one candidate, the official said, while others can make up their own minds. Behind the scenes, the candidates have lobbied their counterparts through letters, face-to-face pitches with NATO ambassadors, at security summits and with phone calls to ministries, said the three officials. Since Berlin nominated Breuer, he has been a frequent visitor to NATO capitals. His recent stops have included Albania, North Macedonia, the U.S., Slovenia, Latvia and Estonia — all in the past two months. Breuer has used trips and meetings with fellow military leaders to make the case for Germany’s candidacy, said a person familiar with the effort. The next military committee chair is expected to take over from Italy’s Adm. Giuseppe Cavo Dragone next July, the same NATO official said.

https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text: Fitness influencer and former reality TV star Sam Wood has appeared in a Queensland court on domestic violence charges. Photograph: Sam Tabone/WireImage View image in fullscreen Fitness influencer and former reality TV star Sam Wood has appeared in a Queensland court on domestic violence charges. Photograph: Sam Tabone/WireImage Queensland Bachelor star Sam Wood denied bail as police allege he choked wife until she ‘thought she would die’ Court hears police attended Wood’s Victorian home over a similar allegation about three years ago, but Snezana Wood had not complained then out of ‘fear of retribution’ Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Ben Smee Thu 8 Oct 2026 01.58 EDT Last modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 07.17 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The wife of former Bachelor star Sam Wood told police she “thought she was going to die” after he allegedly choked and assaulted her, a Queensland court heard on Thursday. The court also heard that police in Victoria had attended Wood’s home in relation to a similar incident about three years ago, but that his wife, Snezana Wood, had not wanted to make a complaint at that time out of “fear of retribution”. Sam Wood, a 46-year-old wellness influencer from Melbourne, was denied bail in a Queensland court on Thursday and will be held in custody indefinitely awaiting trial, after police argued his behaviour was “escalating” and that he posed an unacceptable risk. Former Bachelor star Sam Wood charged with domestic violence Read more Wood appeared in court via video link from the Maroochydore police watch house cells, where he had been held for about four days. He was arrested at Noosa on the Sunshine Coast on Sunday and charged with two domestic violence offences: assault occasioning bodily harm and strangulation in a domestic setting. In outlining the prosecution case, police prosecutor Jeanette Grigoris said the brief of evidence included a triple zero call made by a family member and photographs of Snezana Wood’s injuries. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Grigoris said Snezana Wood was supportive of the charges proceeding. Sam Wood’s lawyer has indicated the reality TV star will fight the charges. The court heard that Snezana Wood alleges she was choked and that “there was a cessation of breath”. “She articulates the banging of her head on the floor. She couldn’t breathe,” Grigoris said. “She thought she was going to die.” Grigoris said Snezana also detailed a previous matter in Victoria “being of a similar nature” and “involved choking”. Sam Wood denied that any previous incident had taken place in Victoria. Grigoris said there was body-worn camera footage of police attending his home and a police report in relation to that incident. Grigoris said Snezana Wood “did not make any criminal complaints on that occasion, she was in fear of retribution of the defendant.” Grigoris also raised concern that Sam Wood, during his police interview, minimised his part in the alleged offending, and minimised the injuries suffered by his wife. “He’s essentially victim blamed,” she said. Sam Wood’s lawyer, Matthew Cuskelly, sought bail and said his client denied the allegations. He cited a psychologist’s report that said Sam Wood was suffering from “severe depression”. “He ought to be given the opportunity to engage with mental health professionals,” Cuskelly said. “And also try to salvage something of his professional reputation and career, which is taking a hell of a beating at the moment. “Ultimately, as all families have, there was problems. And my client had been enduring the hardship of attempting to quarantine those problems from his family for some period of time. It was agonising.” Cuskelly cited a psychologist’s report that describes ‘the difficulty that my client has been enduring in respect of the deterioration of his psychological state”. “His depression is regarded as extremely severe.” Cuskelly said Sam Wood had no prior criminal history and if granted bail would reside in Victoria with his father, Andrew Wood, who attended the court in support of his son. Acting magistrate Janelle Boegheim said she was not satisfied by the defence argument that the case against Sam Wood was weak. “The strength of the evidence against the defendant is … relatively strong at this juncture.” Boegheim said it was likely the charges, if proven, would attract a term in prison. Sam Wood was stood down by his own fitness empire, 28 by Sam Wood, on Monday, a day after he was charged. “We have all been shocked and saddened by the matters involving Sam Wood,” said Mark Watkin, the group’s acting chief executive. “We have zero tolerance for domestic violence. While the matter is under investigation and before the court, Sam is on indefinite leave from his duties. “Our thoughts are with the family and anyone in the community affected by domestic violence.” He is due to face court again on November 23.
